notes.definition: Contraception is the deliberate prevention of pregnancy. Fertility can be controlled by hormonal methods, which stop eggs maturing or being released, and by non-hormonal methods, which stop sperm reaching an egg, kill sperm, or prevent an embryo implanting.
explanation: Hormonal methods change the levels of reproductive hormones. Oral contraceptives (the pill) contain hormones that inhibit FSH production, so no eggs mature. An injection, implant or skin patch releases progesterone slowly. This inhibits the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years, depending on the method. Some intrauterine devices (IUDs) also release a hormone.

Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent sperm reaching an egg. A male condom is worn over the penis; a diaphragm is a flexible cap placed over the cervix. Condoms are the only method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm. They are not very effective on their own, so they are often used with a diaphragm.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are small T-shaped devices placed in the uterus by a doctor or nurse. They prevent the implantation of an embryo, or release a hormone. They can stay in place for several years. Abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct (around ovulation) is a natural method, but it is unreliable because the timing of ovulation can vary and sperm can survive for several days.

Surgical methods of male and female sterilisation involve cutting or tying the tubes that carry gametes: the sperm ducts in men or the oviducts in women. Sterilisation is very effective but should be considered permanent, as it is difficult or impossible to reverse.

You need to evaluate methods. Useful criteria are: how effective the method is, whether it must be remembered daily or lasts for years, side effects (hormonal methods can cause mood changes, weight change or a small increased risk of blood clots), whether it protects against STIs, whether it is reversible, and whether it needs a medical procedure. Religious or personal beliefs can also affect choice.
keyFacts: The oral contraceptive pill contains hormones that inhibit FSH production, so no eggs mature.
Progesterone injections, implants and skin patches inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for months or years.
Condoms and diaphragms are barrier methods that prevent sperm reaching an egg.
Condoms are the only method that also protects against STIs.
IUDs prevent implantation of an embryo or release a hormone.
Spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm.
Abstinence when an egg may be in the oviduct is a natural, non-hormonal method.
Sterilisation cuts or ties the oviducts or sperm ducts and is effectively permanent.
Hormonal methods can have side effects; non-hormonal barrier methods do not.

keyTerms.definition: A pill containing hormones that inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature.
A method, such as a condom or diaphragm, that physically prevents sperm reaching an egg.
A small device placed in the uterus that prevents implantation of an embryo or releases a hormone.
A chemical that kills or disables sperm.
A surgical method in which the oviducts (female) or sperm ducts (male) are cut or tied.
When an embryo attaches into the thick lining of the uterus.

workedExamples.title: Using effectiveness data
workedExamples.question: A contraceptive method is 99 % effective, meaning 1 in 100 women using it for a year becomes pregnant. 2500 women use it for a year. How many pregnancies would be expected?

workedExamples.title: Comparing two methods
workedExamples.question: With typical use, the pill is about 91 % effective and male condoms about 82 % effective. For 1000 couples using each method for a year, how many more pregnancies would be expected with condoms?
workedExamples.answer: About 90 more pregnancies with condoms. A full evaluation would also mention that condoms protect against STIs and have no hormonal side effects.

workedExamples.title: Explaining how a method works
workedExamples.question: Explain how a contraceptive implant prevents pregnancy.
steps: The implant releases progesterone slowly into the blood.
Progesterone inhibits the maturation and release of eggs.
No egg is released, so there is no egg for sperm to fertilise.
It works for a number of years, so it does not need to be remembered daily.
workedExamples.answer: Slow-release progesterone stops eggs maturing and being released, for years.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all contraceptives protect against sexually transmitted infections.
misconceptions.right: In fact only condoms (barrier methods that cover the penis or line the vagina) protect against STIs. The pill, implant and IUD do not.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the contraceptive pill kills sperm.
misconceptions.right: In fact the pill contains hormones that inhibit FSH so no eggs mature. Spermicides kill or disable sperm.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sterilisation is easily reversed.
misconceptions.right: In fact sterilisation should be thought of as permanent; reversal is difficult and often unsuccessful.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an egg is always released on day 14, so avoiding sex then is reliable.
misconceptions.right: In fact ovulation varies between cycles and sperm can survive for several days, so abstinence methods are unreliable.

realWorld: Long-acting methods such as implants and IUDs are recommended to people who may forget to take a daily pill.
Free condoms are offered by sexual health services to reduce the spread of STIs such as chlamydia and HIV.
Some people avoid hormonal methods because of side effects or for religious reasons, and choose natural or barrier methods instead.
examTips: For each method, learn one line on how it works: stops eggs maturing, stops eggs being released, stops sperm reaching the egg, kills sperm, or stops implantation.
Say 'inhibits FSH so no eggs mature' for the pill. Vague answers like 'stops you getting pregnant' score nothing.
In 'evaluate' questions give advantages AND disadvantages of each method, then a justified conclusion that fits the person in the question.
When given effectiveness data, use it: quote figures and calculate expected pregnancies if asked.
summary: Contraception can be hormonal or non-hormonal.
The pill inhibits FSH so no eggs mature.
Progesterone injections, implants and patches stop eggs maturing and being released for months or years.
Condoms and diaphragms stop sperm reaching the egg; condoms also protect against STIs.
IUDs prevent implantation or release a hormone; spermicides kill or disable sperm.
Abstinence around ovulation and surgical sterilisation are other methods.
Evaluate using effectiveness, side effects, convenience, STI protection and reversibility.

flashcards.front: How does the oral contraceptive pill work?

flashcards.front: How do progesterone injections, implants and patches work?
flashcards.back: Slow release of progesterone inhibits the maturation and release of eggs for months or years.

flashcards.front: How do condoms and diaphragms work?
flashcards.back: They are barriers that prevent sperm reaching an egg.
They prevent implantation of an embryo or release a hormone.
Avoiding intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct (around ovulation).

flashcards.front: Give two disadvantages of the pill.
flashcards.back: Side effects (e.g. mood or weight changes, blood clot risk), must remember daily, no STI protection.

questions.question: How does a condom prevent pregnancy?
options: It prevents sperm reaching the egg
markScheme: 1 mark: It prevents sperm reaching the egg
questions.explanation: A condom is a barrier method. Spermicides kill sperm, hormonal methods stop eggs being released and IUDs prevent implantation.

questions.question: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections?
markScheme: 1 mark: Condom
questions.explanation: Condoms stop body fluids passing between partners, so they reduce the spread of STIs. The other methods do not provide a barrier.

questions.question: What do spermicidal agents do?
markScheme: 1 mark: Kill or disable sperm
questions.explanation: Spermicides are chemicals that kill or disable sperm. They are not very effective on their own so are often used with a diaphragm.

questions.question: Which of these is a surgical method of contraception?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sterilisation
questions.explanation: Sterilisation involves surgery to cut or tie the oviducts or sperm ducts. An implant is inserted under the skin in a minor procedure but is a hormonal method, not surgical sterilisation.

questions.question: How does the oral contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
options: It inhibits LH so the uterus lining breaks down
It contains hormones that inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
It kills sperm in the vagina
markScheme: 1 mark: It contains hormones that inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
questions.explanation: FSH is needed for an egg to mature. Without it, no egg is ready for release, so fertilisation cannot happen.

questions.question: Which of these is a hormonal method of contraception?
markScheme: 1 mark: Contraceptive implant
questions.explanation: The implant releases progesterone slowly. A diaphragm is a barrier, a copper IUD prevents implantation without hormones and spermicide is a chemical that kills sperm.

questions.question: Which hormone is released slowly by a contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch?
markScheme: 1 mark: Progesterone
questions.explanation: Slow-release progesterone inhibits the maturation and release of eggs for months or years. FSH and LH would promote egg maturation and release.

questions.question: What happens in female sterilisation?
options: A cap is placed over the cervix
The oviducts are cut or tied
markScheme: 1 mark: The oviducts are cut or tied
questions.explanation: Cutting or tying the oviducts stops eggs and sperm meeting. The ovaries still work and the menstrual cycle continues.

questions.question: Where is a diaphragm placed?
options: Under the skin of the arm
markScheme: 1 mark: Over the cervix
questions.explanation: A diaphragm is a barrier that covers the cervix so sperm cannot enter the uterus. An IUD goes inside the uterus; an implant goes under the skin.

questions.question: Why is avoiding intercourse around the expected time of ovulation an unreliable method of contraception?
options: Sperm only survive for a few minutes
The day of ovulation can vary from one cycle to the next
The uterus lining is always thick enough for implantation
markScheme: 1 mark: The day of ovulation can vary from one cycle to the next
questions.explanation: Cycles vary in length, so ovulation is hard to predict. Sperm can also survive for several days, so intercourse before ovulation can still lead to fertilisation.

questions.question: How does an intrauterine device (IUD) that does not release hormones prevent pregnancy?
options: It stops eggs maturing in the ovary
It prevents implantation of an embryo
markScheme: 1 mark: It prevents implantation of an embryo
questions.explanation: The specification describes IUDs as preventing implantation of an embryo or releasing a hormone. Only hormonal methods inhibit FSH or stop eggs maturing.

questions.question: A woman often forgets to take tablets. Which is the best reason for her to choose a contraceptive implant rather than the pill?
options: The implant has no possible side effects
The implant works for years without needing to be remembered each day
markScheme: 1 mark: The implant works for years without needing to be remembered each day
questions.explanation: Missing pills reduces effectiveness. The implant still releases hormones so can have side effects, and it does not protect against STIs or kill sperm.

questions.question: Name two barrier methods of contraception.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: male condom; female condom; diaphragm
questions.explanation: Barrier methods physically stop sperm reaching an egg.

questions.question: Give one advantage of using a condom rather than the contraceptive pill.
markScheme: 1 mark: protects against sexually transmitted infections / no hormonal side effects / only needed at the time of intercourse
questions.explanation: The key advantage examiners look for is STI protection. Condoms also have no hormonal side effects.

questions.question: Explain how a contraceptive implant prevents pregnancy.
markScheme: 1 mark: releases progesterone slowly (over months or years)
1 mark: inhibits the maturation and release of eggs
questions.explanation: No mature egg is released, so fertilisation cannot occur. Its long-lasting action is why it is useful for people who forget daily pills.

questions.question: Give two disadvantages of the oral contraceptive pill.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: possible side effects (e.g. mood changes, weight change, increased risk of blood clots); must be remembered every day; does not protect against STIs
questions.explanation: Each disadvantage must be specific. 'It can go wrong' is too vague; 'less effective if a pill is missed' is acceptable.

questions.question: Explain why sterilisation is only recommended for people who are sure they do not want any more children.
markScheme: 1 mark: sterilisation is (usually) permanent / very difficult to reverse
1 mark: because the oviducts or sperm ducts are cut, so eggs and sperm cannot meet
questions.explanation: Once the tubes are cut or tied, gametes cannot meet. Reversal surgery is difficult and often unsuccessful.

questions.question: Explain how abstaining from intercourse at certain times of the menstrual cycle can prevent pregnancy.
markScheme: 1 mark: no intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct (around ovulation)
1 mark: so sperm are not present to fertilise the egg
questions.explanation: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct. If there are no sperm there when an egg is present, fertilisation cannot happen.

questions.question: The combined pill contains oestrogen and progesterone. Explain why taking this pill stops eggs maturing.
markScheme: 1 mark: the hormones in the pill keep oestrogen/progesterone levels high
1 mark: this inhibits FSH release from the pituitary gland
1 mark: FSH is needed for an egg to mature, so no egg matures (and none is released)
questions.explanation: This links contraception to the Higher tier interactions in the menstrual cycle: oestrogen and progesterone both inhibit FSH.

questions.question: Suggest why a spermicide is usually used together with a diaphragm rather than on its own.
markScheme: 1 mark: spermicide on its own is not very effective
1 mark: used together, spermicide kills/disables any sperm that get past the diaphragm, so the combination is more effective
questions.explanation: Two methods working in different ways give a higher overall effectiveness than either alone.

questions.question: In a study, 200 couples used a contraceptive method for one year. 4 of the women became pregnant. Calculate the percentage of women who became pregnant.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 2 %
questions.explanation: 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02, × 100 = 2 %. So the method was 98 % effective in this study.

questions.question: A contraceptive injection lasts for 13 weeks. How many injections would a woman need in 52 weeks?
markScheme: 1 mark: = 4
questions.explanation: 52 ÷ 13 = 4. Needing only 4 injections a year is an advantage over a daily pill.

questions.question: A contraceptive method is 99 % effective: 1 in every 100 women using it for a year becomes pregnant. Calculate the number of pregnancies expected if 2500 women use this method for one year.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1 % of women become pregnant
questions.explanation: 100 − 99 = 1 % failure rate. 1 % of 2500 is 25. A common error is to calculate 99 % of 2500 (2475), which is the number who do not become pregnant.

questions.question: With typical use, the pill is 91 % effective and male condoms are 82 % effective. 1000 couples use each method for a year. Calculate how many more pregnancies would be expected among the couples using condoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: pill 9 % of 1000 = 90; condoms 18 % of 1000 = 180
questions.explanation: Convert effectiveness to failure rate first (100 − effectiveness), then find the number of pregnancies for each and subtract.

questions.question: Method A: 6 of 750 women became pregnant in a year. Method B: 9 of 1200 women became pregnant in a year. Calculate the effectiveness of method B as a percentage (the percentage of women who did NOT become pregnant). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9 ÷ 1200 × 100 = 0.75 % pregnant
questions.explanation: Method A: 6 ÷ 750 = 0.8 % pregnant (99.2 % effective). Method B is slightly more effective at 99.25 %, even though more women became pregnant, because the sample was larger. Always compare percentages, not raw numbers.

questions.question: Describe how hormonal methods of contraception prevent pregnancy.
markScheme: Indicative content: oral contraceptives contain hormones; these inhibit FSH production; so no eggs mature; injections, implants and skin patches release progesterone slowly; progesterone inhibits the maturation and release of eggs; these last for a number of months or years; some IUDs release a hormone; with no egg released, fertilisation cannot occur.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two hormonal methods described with correct hormone action (FSH inhibition or progesterone stopping maturation and release).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): methods named with limited or vague description of how they work.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Name the method, the hormone and its effect. 'Stops eggs maturing' for the pill and 'stops maturation and release of eggs' for progesterone methods are the key phrases.

questions.question: Describe how non-hormonal methods of contraception prevent pregnancy.
markScheme: Indicative content: condoms (male and female) are barriers preventing sperm reaching the egg; diaphragm covers the cervix as a barrier; condoms also protect against STIs; spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm; often used with a diaphragm; copper IUD prevents implantation of an embryo; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; female sterilisation cuts or ties the oviducts; male sterilisation cuts or ties the sperm ducts; sterilisation stops eggs and sperm meeting.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): at least four non-hormonal methods, each with a correct, clear explanation of how it prevents pregnancy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two or three methods with correct descriptions, or more methods with limited description.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): methods named with little or no description.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Cover a range: barriers, chemical (spermicide), IUD, natural method and surgery. Each needs a 'how it works' clause.

questions.question: A couple want to avoid pregnancy for the next two years and then try for a baby. Evaluate the use of the contraceptive pill, condoms and sterilisation for this couple.
markScheme: Indicative content, pill: very effective if taken correctly; reversible, fertility returns soon after stopping; inhibits FSH so no eggs mature; but must be taken daily, side effects (mood, weight, blood clots), no STI protection.
Condoms: no hormonal side effects; protect against STIs; easily available; reversible immediately; but less effective with typical use (may split or be used incorrectly); must be used every time.
Sterilisation: very effective; but effectively permanent and difficult to reverse; requires surgery; unsuitable because they want a baby in two years.
Conclusion: e.g. pill (or a long-acting reversible method) is most suitable for effectiveness and reversibility; condoms useful if STI protection matters; sterilisation not suitable.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): advantages and disadvantages of all three methods linked to the couple's needs, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods; conclusion may be weak.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or more methods.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers apply each point to this couple, especially reversibility, and make a clear final choice with a reason.
